Assignment 01 / Sculpting for Design

Tactile Topographies

I collected surfaces from the everyday world and translated them into the language of clay.

Observation · Sketching · Clay

I started by looking closely at textures around me, then explored how I could suggest their surfaces and the feelings they evoked through sketches and clay.

01

Looking a little closer

I began by observing natural and man-made textures in my surroundings. Bark, ground cover, patterned paving, and geometric surfaces became a small library of marks. I looked at the contrast between regular, constructed patterns and uneven surfaces shaped by growth.

My photographs became starting points rather than patterns to reproduce exactly. I could pick out lines, ridges, gaps, and small interruptions, then think about how to translate them into another material.

02

From surface to mark

I translated my observations into sketches, exploring hatching, dots, repeated curves, and other ways of describing a surface. Drawing helped me separate a texture from the object it belonged to.

I also put together a visual collection of textures. These studies helped me move from noticing a surface to choosing which qualities I could carry into clay.

03

A surface you can hold

In my clay model, I tried to suggest water leaving its marks on a riverbed, the bark of a tree, and the roughness of moss and small pebbles. I brought several of these textures together on one curved form.

I worked around the vessel so that different textures could sit beside one another. Broad channels contrast with smaller impressions, while a rough band near the rim connects the surfaces below it. The different views show how the marks continue around the form.

04

Observed, then imagined

I also experimented with hatching and dots to create imaginary textures. I used what I had observed as a starting point, then combined and extended those marks in clay.

I wanted to explore how a familiar sensation — flowing water, rough bark, or pebbled ground — could be suggested through a different material. The final object brings observation and experimentation together.
